title: Symmetry and Periodicity
short: sin(−θ) = −sin θ, cos(−θ) = cos θ, and both repeat every 2π.

blocks.html: Two simple moves on the unit circle explain a lot about sine and cosine: reflecting across the $x$-axis, and going all the way around. Both build on reference angles.

Symmetry. The angle $-\theta$ turns the same amount the other way, so its point is the reflection of $(x, y)$ across the $x$-axis: $(x, -y)$. The $x$-coordinate stays, so cosine is even; the $y$-coordinate flips, so sine is odd.
Periodicity. Adding $2\pi$ is one more full turn, which lands on the same point, so every value repeats. Adding only $\pi$ sends $(x, y)$ to the opposite point $(-x, -y)$; both signs flip, and the ratio $\frac{y}{x}$ does not change. That is why tangent repeats every $\pi$.

blocks.title: Using the period
steps: $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ is in Quadrant II with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$: $\cos\frac{5\pi}{6} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

blocks.title: Without knowing the angle
steps: A half turn sends the point to the opposite side of the circle: $\cos(\theta + \pi) = -0.6$.

blocks.html: Writing $\cos(-\theta) = -\cos\theta$, treating every trig function like sine. Check with $\theta = 0$: $\cos 0 = 1$, and $\cos(-0)$ is also $1$, not $-1$.
A function with $f(x + p) = f(x)$ for all $x$ is periodic, and the smallest such $p > 0$ is its period: $2\pi$ for sine and cosine, $\pi$ for tangent.
